cards.title: Your digital keys
cards.body:
Every account you have, from games to school to email, is locked with a **password**. It's the key to your stuff.

Some keys are easy to copy, and some are almost impossible. In this lesson you'll learn what makes a password strong, and how to make one you can actually remember.

cards.title: How passwords get guessed
cards.body:
When a website gets hacked, the stolen passwords are often scrambled so they can't just be read. So attackers use computers to **guess** them, billions of times a second.

They start with the **most common passwords** (like `password123` and `qwerty`), real words, names, birthdays and patterns like swapping `a` for `@`. Those fall almost instantly.

A truly random password has to be found the slow way: trying **every combination**. For lowercase letters, each position could be any of 26 letters, so every extra letter makes the job **26 times bigger**.

cards.prompt: Is each password **easy to guess** or **hard to guess**?

items.label: Your pet's name and birth year
A long random one made by a password app

cards.explanation: Common passwords, keyboard patterns, names, birthdays and swaps like `@` for `a` are the **first things guessed**. Several random words, or a long random password made by an app, have to be found by trying every combination.
cards.hint: Think about what guessers try first: common passwords, patterns, names and birthdays, and swaps like @ for a.
cards.nudge: Swapping letters for symbols (`@`, `0`) doesn't fool a guessing computer. It tries those swaps early on.

cards.prompt: This password uses only **lowercase letters**. Make it long enough that trying every combination would take **at least 100 years**.
cards.explanation: Each extra letter multiplies the combinations by 26. Eight letters fall in minutes, but **14 lowercase letters** would take a fast computer thousands of years to try. Length is what makes a password strong.
cards.hint: Slide the length up one letter at a time and watch the time grow. Every letter makes it 26 times longer.
cards.nudge: Keep going: a few more letters make a huge difference, because each one multiplies the time by 26.

cards.title: Length wins
cards.body:
Adding capitals, numbers and symbols gives a guesser more characters to try, which helps a little. Making a password **longer** helps a lot more.

The easiest way to get length you can remember is a **passphrase**: **four or more random words**, at least **15 characters** long, like `violet cactus harbour pepper`. That's what Australia's cyber security experts at cyber.gov.au recommend.

The words must be **random**. A song lyric, a famous quote or your pet's name is easy to guess, however long it is.

cards.prompt: Now the password can be **10 characters at most**. Reach **100 years** anyway, by choosing which kinds of characters it can use.
cards.explanation: Mixing in capitals, numbers and symbols means more characters to choose from, so a **short random** password can reach 100 years too. But it's hard to remember. That's why long passphrases, or a password manager, work better for people.
cards.hint: At 10 characters, lowercase alone isn't enough. Turn on more kinds of characters and watch how many there are to choose from.
cards.nudge: Push the length to 10, then add kinds of characters until the time passes 100 years.

cards.prompt: Which of these makes the **best** passphrase?

options.nudge: Song lyrics and famous lines are in guessing lists. The words need to be random, not ones that belong together.
Pet names and birth years are easy for someone to find out or guess. Look for words with no link to you or to each other.
Swapping letters for symbols is one of the first tricks a guesser tries, and it's short. Look for length made of random words.

cards.explanation: Four **random, unrelated** words give length that's easy to remember and hard to guess. Lyrics, personal details and symbol swaps are all tried early by guessing computers.
cards.hint: Look for four or more words that have nothing to do with each other, or with you.

cards.title: One password per account
cards.body:
Websites sometimes get hacked, and their list of email addresses and passwords is stolen. This is a [[data breach]].

Attackers then try that same email and password on **other** websites. If you used it everywhere, one breach opens every account.

So every account needs its **own** password. If one leaks, change it everywhere you used it, starting with your **email**: it can reset the passwords of all your other accounts.

Nobody can remember dozens of strong passwords, and you don't have to: a [[password manager]] can remember them for you. More on that next lesson.

cards.prompt: You get an email from a game website: it was hacked, and passwords were stolen.

steps.text: You used the **same password** for that game and for your email account. What do you do first?

choices.text: Change your email password to a new, unique one
choices.consequence: Good. Your email is the most important account: it can reset all the others.

choices.text: Nothing. It's only a game account
choices.consequence: The same password opens your email too. Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites.
The stolen password still opens your email. That's the one to change first.

steps.text: Your email is safe again. What about the game account?

choices.text: Give it its own new password too
choices.consequence: Now each account has its own password, so one leak can't open the other.

choices.text: Use your new email password for the game as well
choices.consequence: Then the next breach could open your email again. Every account needs its own password.

cards.explanation: One stolen password shouldn't open two accounts. Change it everywhere you used it, starting with your **email**, which can reset everything else, and give every account its own password.
cards.hint: Think about which account could be used to reset all your others. Then think about why every account needs its own password.

cards.prompt: A password is just **2 lowercase letters** long. How many different combinations could it be?
cards.explanation: Each position could be any of 26 letters: 26 × 26 = **676**. A computer tries all of those in a blink. Every extra letter multiplies it by 26 again, which is why length matters so much.
cards.hint: Each of the two positions could be any of 26 letters. How many pairs is that?
cards.nudge: Multiply the choices for each position: 26 for the first letter, and 26 for the second.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Guessers try **common passwords, words, names and patterns** first.
- **Length** matters most: each extra lowercase letter makes it 26 times harder.
- A **passphrase** is four or more **random** words, at least 15 characters.
- Give every account its **own** password, so one [[data breach]] can't open the rest.

Next: a second lock on the door, and an app that remembers passwords for you.
